prompt: What does the Wolff–Kishner reaction, treatment of an aldehyde or ketone with hydrazine (H2N–NH2) and KOH, accomplish?

choices.text: It converts the C=O group into CH2, giving an alkane: R2C=O → R2CH2
It converts the C=O group into CH–OH, giving an alcohol
choices.why: Alcohols come from hydride reduction. The Wolff–Kishner reaction removes the oxygen completely.

choices.text: It converts the C=O group into C=N–NH2, giving a hydrazone as the final product
choices.why: The hydrazone is only an intermediate; with base it loses N2 and gives the alkane.

choices.text: It converts the C=O group into C=CH2, giving an alkene
choices.why: Alkenes come from the Wittig reaction (Section 19.11). Wolff–Kishner gives an alkane.

explanation: The Wolff–Kishner reaction is a useful and general method for converting an aldehyde or ketone into an alkane, R2C=O → R2CH2, by treatment with hydrazine in the presence of KOH.

prompt: Propiophenone, C6H5COCH2CH3, is treated with hydrazine and KOH. What organic product forms?

choices.why: That's a hydride reduction product. Wolff–Kishner removes the oxygen completely, giving CH2.
No carbon is lost. The C=O carbon stays in the chain as a CH2 group.
The hydrazone is an intermediate; with KOH it goes on to lose N2.

explanation: In the Wolff–Kishner reaction the C=O group becomes CH2. Propiophenone gives propylbenzene, along with N2 and water.

prompt: Cyclopropanecarbaldehyde, C3H5CHO (formula C4H6O), is treated with hydrazine and KOH. How many hydrogen atoms does the hydrocarbon product contain?
explanation: R2C=O → R2CH2: the oxygen is removed and the carbonyl carbon gains two hydrogens. C4H6O becomes C4H8, methylcyclopropane.

prompt: What is the first intermediate formed in the Wolff–Kishner reaction?

choices.why: Cyanohydrins form from HCN. Hydrazine, like a primary amine, gives an imine-type product, a hydrazone.
Gem diols come from water. Hydrazine first gives a hydrazone.
Enamines come from secondary amines. Hydrazine's NH2 group forms a C=N bond, like a primary amine.

explanation: The Wolff–Kishner reaction is a variant of imine formation. It involves formation of a hydrazone intermediate, R2C=N–NH2, followed by base-catalyzed double-bond migration, loss of N2 gas to give a carbanion, and protonation to give the alkane.

prompt: In step 2 of the Wolff–Kishner mechanism, base removes a weakly acidic N–H proton to give a hydrazone anion. Where does its allylic resonance structure place the double bond and the negative charge?

choices.text: The double bond between the two nitrogens and the negative charge on carbon
The double bond between carbon and nitrogen and the negative charge on oxygen
choices.why: The oxygen is already gone, lost as water when the hydrazone formed.

choices.text: A triple bond between the nitrogens and a positive charge on carbon
choices.why: The N≡N triple bond appears only when N2 is released later. The anion's resonance form has N=N and a carbon anion.

choices.text: A carbon–carbon double bond and the negative charge on nitrogen
choices.why: The resonance form that matters puts the double bond between the nitrogens and the negative charge on carbon.

explanation: The hydrazone anion has an allylic resonance structure that places the double bond between the nitrogens and the negative charge on carbon. Reprotonation then occurs on carbon, giving the double-bond rearrangement product.

prompt: What drives the loss of nitrogen and formation of an alkyl anion in the Wolff–Kishner reaction?

choices.text: The large thermodynamic stability of the N2 molecule
The release of water from the hydrazone
choices.why: Water is lost earlier, when the hydrazone forms.

choices.text: Oxidation of the carbon by KOH
choices.why: KOH is a base, not an oxidizing agent.

choices.text: The high acidity of the alkane C–H bonds
choices.why: The step is driven by forming N2, not by any acidic C–H bond.

explanation: The step in which nitrogen is lost and an alkyl anion forms is driven by the large thermodynamic stability of the N2 molecule. The anion is then protonated to give the alkane.

prompt: Counting hydrazone formation as step 1 and the final protonation as the last step, how many steps does the Wolff–Kishner mechanism have?
explanation: Five (Figure 19.9.1): (1) hydrazone formation, (2) deprotonation of N–H to the resonance-stabilized anion, (3) protonation on carbon, (4) deprotonation with loss of N2 to give a carbanion, and (5) protonation to the alkane.

prompt: Why is the Wolff–Kishner reduction more general than catalytic hydrogenation of an acylbenzene to an alkylbenzene?

choices.text: It works well with both alkyl and aryl ketones
It works only with aryl ketones
choices.why: Being limited to acylbenzenes is the drawback of the hydrogenation route. Wolff–Kishner also works with alkyl ketones.

choices.text: It gives an alcohol instead of an alkane
choices.why: Both routes give the same overall change, C=O to CH2.
The Wolff–Kishner reaction uses KOH as the base.

explanation: The Wolff–Kishner reduction accomplishes the same overall transformation as catalytic hydrogenation of an acylbenzene to an alkylbenzene (Section 16.9), but it is more general and more useful because it works well with both alkyl and aryl ketones.

prompt: 4-Methyl-3-penten-2-one, (CH3)2C=CHCOCH3, is treated with N2H4 and KOH. What is the product?

choices.why: The Wolff–Kishner reaction changes only the C=O group. Saturating the C=C bond would also take H2/Pd.
This is what H2/Pd gives: the C=C bond is reduced and the ketone is kept.
An alcohol would come from hydride reduction. Wolff–Kishner turns C=O into CH2.

explanation: Hydrazine and KOH convert the C=O group into CH2 and leave the C=C bond in place, giving 2-methyl-2-pentene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3 (Exercise 19.9.1).

choices.why: This removes the carbonyl oxygen but leaves the C=C bond, giving 2-methyl-2-pentene.
This reduces the C=C bond but leaves the ketone, giving 4-methyl-2-pentanone.
This reduces the ketone to an alcohol; the oxygen stays in the product.

explanation: Two changes are needed: H2/Pd saturates the C=C bond, and the Wolff–Kishner reaction (N2H4, KOH) turns C=O into CH2. Together they give 2-methylpentane (Exercise 19.9.1).
